frames.narration: The crawler has seen 1 billion URLs. Stored exactly at about 100 bytes each that is 100 GB, so every check would be a lookup on disk. A Bloom filter with 9.6 bits per URL is 1.2 GB and fits in memory.
A page links to /pricing. The filter hashes it with 7 hash functions to 7 bit positions. One of those bits is 0, so /pricing was definitely never added: no store lookup is needed.
The crawler queues /pricing and sets its 7 bits to 1. Bits are only ever set, never cleared, so every later check of /pricing finds all 7 set: a Bloom filter has no false negatives.
/about was crawled yesterday. All 7 of its bits are 1, so the answer is 'probably seen' and the link is skipped, again without touching the 100 GB store.

/careers is new, but other URLs happen to have set all 7 of its bits: a false positive. At 1%, 1 in 100 new URLs looks seen, so of 50 million new links a day about 500,000 would be skipped. Where that matters, confirm 'probably seen' in the store: a false positive then costs one extra lookup.

To recrawl /about later, the crawler cannot clear its 7 bits: other URLs share them and would start to look new. A counting Bloom filter keeps a 4-bit counter per slot so items can be removed, at 4 times the memory: 4.8 GB.

To count distinct URLs found today, each crawler shard keeps a HyperLogLog: 16,384 registers of 6 bits, 12 KB. It hashes each URL, picks a register with the first 14 bits and keeps the longest run of leading zeros in the rest.

The stats service merges the two sketches by keeping the larger value in each register, like Redis PFMERGE. A URL found by both shards counts once. The estimate is about 50 million, typically within 0.81% (about 405,000), from 12 KB instead of a 5 GB list.

To find the most-linked hosts, a count-min sketch adds 1 to one counter in each of 4 rows. news.example truly has 2,400 links; its counters read 2,412, 2,400, 2,455 and 2,403 because other hosts share some. The smallest, 2,400, is the estimate: it can be too high, never too low.
